question: An increasingly worrying trend is being seen at the German-Swiss border in BadenWürttemberg. Swiss farmers are farming agricultural land in Germany from their place of business in Switzerland, and, for these areas located in the EU, they receive direct EU funding, even though their actual farmsteads, stables and central operating facilities are located in a non-EU country. This creates serious problems in enforcing EU standards and puts the financial interests of the Union at risk. 1.
What does the Commission make of this unequal treatment at the EU’s external borders?

Does it agree that the fact that it is impossible to conduct on-the-spot checks at the Swiss farmsteads or enforce any recovery claims in a third country is contrary to Article 59 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 on the protection of the financial interests of the Union?

What measures will it take to ensure that in future EU agricultural aid to third-country nationals is conditional upon them having a place of business (branch) within the EU that is fully subject to inspection and sanctions?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.11.2026) Swiss farmers are allowed to farm agricultural land in Germany and may receive Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) support if they have established a registered holding in the country and comply with EU rules.

The current rules1 require a clear and unambiguous identification of beneficiaries, therefore the farmer has to register the farm in the Member State where the support is claimed. There cannot be unequal treatment as CAP rules apply independently from the place of residence of the farmer. Other rules such as taxation, social security are not harmonised within the EU and third countries.

In principle controls operated on the land by the Member States are possible as the agricultural land is in the EU. However, the Member States may reject an aid application or payment claim if the beneficiary or his representative prevents an on-the-spot check from being carried out e.g. in the farmstead outside the EU.

Any non-compliance determines the recovery as regards the ‘registered farm’, independent of the place of residence of the farmer. In the proposal for future CAP, that is being discussed with co-legislators and hence is subject to possible changes, the Commission has not proposed any specific rule for third country residents.
It will be for the Member States, under their National Plans, to define the interventions, the eligibility conditions and the level of support for each specific intervention.
